actions.justification: Mandatory first step — continuous monitoring of HR, BP, SpO2, RR to assess hemodynamic stability and severity of presentation in a patient with suspected PE.
Mandatory — Wells criteria for PE must be calculated to determine pre-test probability and guide the diagnostic workup (D-dimer vs. direct imaging).
Mandatory — D-dimer is a key diagnostic step for PE workup. If Wells score is low/intermediate, a negative D-dimer can rule out PE without imaging.

AHA Class I recommendation: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of presentation for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI and assess for signs of right heart strain (S1Q3T3 pattern) consistent with pulmonary embolism. Patient arrived 15 minutes ago and ECG has not yet been obtained.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. While SpO2 is currently 98%, supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care during initial assessment of suspected PE to maintain oxygenation reserve, especially given the acute presentation.

Chest X-ray is part of the standard initial assessment for acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and is recommended in PE workup guidelines.

Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction, which is critical for risk stratification of suspected pulmonary embolism and guides management decisions (e.g., thrombolysis vs. anticoagulation alone).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, high suspicion for pulmonary embolism. CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard for PE diagnosis. Wells score and D-dimer have already been assessed; CT-PA is the next step to confirm PE, especially important given HIT history which will affect anticoagulation choice.

12-lead ECG should be obtained per AHA guidelines within 10 minutes of chest pain presentation to evaluate for STEMI or other cardiac causes. Although order_ecg was done, order_imaging_ecg is a distinct action_id in the available list and should be completed to ensure full cardiac workup including S1Q3T3 pattern or right heart strain suggestive of PE.

Given suspected pulmonary embolism with known heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), pulmonology consultation is warranted to assist in management decisions, particularly regarding non-heparin anticoagulation strategies (e.g., argatroban or fondaparinux) and further workup.
ABG is indicated to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with suspected PE workup.
Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound to evaluate for DVT, which would support PE diagnosis and inform anticoagulation urgency.

Patient has HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) as a comorbidity — anticoagulation with a non-heparin agent (e.g., argatroban or fondaparinux) is indicated for suspected PE. NOTE: heparin and LMWH are contraindicated given HIT history; this action represents appropriate non-heparin anticoagulation.
CBC is needed to assess baseline platelet count given known HIT history, and to evaluate for anemia or infection contributing to dyspnea. This is not yet completed.
BMP provides renal function data critical for anticoagulation dosing decisions (especially non-heparin alternatives given HIT) and electrolyte status in this dyspneic patient.
BNP helps assess for right heart strain or heart failure contributing to dyspnea, particularly relevant if CT-PA confirms PE causing right ventricular pressure overload.
Troponin is essential to assess right ventricular strain and myocardial injury in suspected PE, helping stratify risk (massive vs submassive). Not yet ordered per completed actions list.

Coagulation studies are critical given this patient's HIT history — baseline PT/INR/aPTT needed to guide selection of alternative anticoagulants (e.g., argatroban or fondaparinux) since heparin and LMWH are contraindicated.
Lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and hemodynamic adequacy. Elevated lactate would indicate hemodynamic compromise and may support escalation of therapy in PE management.

Patient has suspected PE with known HIT, making standard heparin/LMWH anticoagulation contraindicated. Interventional radiology consultation is appropriate to evaluate for catheter-directed thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy as alternative treatment strategies for PE in the setting of HIT.

Bedside echocardiogram to assess RV size and function for PE risk stratification. Patient has suspected PE with HIT - echo findings will guide anticoagulation strategy (e.g., argatroban or fondaparinux as alternatives to heparin/LMWH) and determine if massive PE requiring escalated therapy is present.

Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with suspected PE. IV fluid support may be indicated to maintain preload in the setting of right heart strain, while awaiting CT-PA results and definitive anticoagulation decisions. Patient is hemodynamically stable (MAP 78) so cautious fluid administration is appropriate.

Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain concerning for PE. With HIT comorbidity, heparin and LMWH are contraindicated. CT-PA has been ordered. Given hemodynamic monitoring needs and potential for deterioration in PE, vasopressor support readiness is warranted. All other available actions (give_heparin, give_lmwh) are contraindicated due to HIT, and thrombolysis is not yet indicated in a hemodynamically stable patient (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%).

Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia), making heparin and LMWH contraindicated. Given the clinical presentation consistent with pulmonary embolism and the contraindication to heparin-based anticoagulation, thrombolysis may be considered if there is evidence of hemodynamic compromise or high-risk PE. Of the three available actions, give_heparin and give_lmwh are contraindicated in HIT. Thrombolysis is the only potentially appropriate option from the available list, though clinical reassessment of severity is warranted.
